title: Binary Search: Find a Target
oneLiner: Cut the search space in half every step -- O(log n) instead of O(n), but only works on sorted data.
keyTakeaway: Binary search only works because the array is sorted: comparing the middle element to the target tells you which HALF the target could possibly be in, so the other half gets thrown away entirely, every single step -- that's exactly what turns a linear scan into O(log n).
explanation: Keep two pointers, left and right, spanning the whole array to start. While left <= right: look at the middle index (left + (right - left) / 2), and compare its value to the target. Equal -- found it, done. Too small -- the target (if present) has to be to the right, so move left to mid + 1. Too big -- it has to be to the left, so move right to mid - 1. Each comparison eliminates HALF the remaining candidates, which is why this takes at most about log2(n) comparisons (the number of times n can be halved before one candidate is left: 20 for a million items) instead of up to n. Watch out for the loop condition being `left <= right`, not `left < right` -- with strict `<` you can stop one comparison too early and miss checking the single remaining candidate when left and right meet.

recognitionSignals: The input is sorted (or you're allowed to sort it) and you need to find a specific value or a boundary.
You need better than O(n) search, and the brute-force approach is an obvious linear scan.
The problem is phrased as "find the smallest/largest X such that some condition holds" -- often solvable by binary searching on the ANSWER itself, not just an array.
gotchas: Loop condition must be `left <= right`, not `left < right` -- with `<` you can miss checking the last remaining candidate.
Update to `mid + 1` / `mid - 1` for the next boundary, not `mid` itself -- reusing mid causes an infinite loop once left and right converge on it.

`(left + right) / 2` can overflow (exceed the largest value the integer type can hold and wrap around) in fixed-width-integer languages on huge arrays -- `left + (right - left) / 2` avoids it. Python ints can't overflow, but a C# `int` is 32-bit, so `left + right` can pass int.MaxValue on very large arrays or wide answer ranges -- that's the reason the safer form exists and shows up in interviews.
confusableWith: Two Pointers (this track) also uses two indices, but moves them toward each other, inspecting values along the way; binary search only ever looks at the midpoint and discards half the remaining space without inspecting it. The tell: do you need to examine a range (two pointers), or can you safely skip most of it based on one comparison (binary search)?

complexity.note: The search range halves every step, so it takes log₂ n steps; only a few index variables are stored.
